title: Tiger Woods Changed Golf Forever — Here's How
summary: Before Tiger Woods, golf was a sport for a specific demographic. After Tiger, it was something else entirely. His impact on the game — in viewership, prize money, athleticism, and global reach — is without parallel in the sport's history.
content:
When Tiger Woods won the 1997 Masters at the age of 21 by 12 strokes — the largest winning margin in the tournament's history — golf changed. Not gradually, not incrementally, but immediately and permanently. The television ratings for that final round were the highest in Masters history. The following week, golf club sales spiked across the United States. And a generation of young people who had never considered golf as something for them began paying attention.

Woods is the most transformative figure in golf's history, and arguably one of the most transformative athletes in the history of any sport. His influence extends far beyond his 15 major championships — extraordinary as that record is.

The Athleticism Revolution

Golf before Woods was not an athletic sport in the traditional sense. Players did not train like athletes. The idea of a golfer having a personal trainer, following a strict diet, working on physical conditioning as seriously as on the golf swing — this was largely foreign to the professional game.

Woods changed all of that. He trained like a Navy SEAL. His physique — powerful, explosive, built for the rotational demands of the golf swing — was unlike anything the tour had seen. And within a decade, every serious professional was training, dieting, and conditioning in ways that would have seemed excessive to the previous generation.

The Tiger Effect on Prize Money

The PGA Tour's total prize money in 1996, the year before Woods turned professional, was approximately $65 million. By 2010, it had risen to over $280 million. The correlation is not coincidental — Woods drove television ratings, which drove broadcast deals, which drove sponsor investment, which drove prize money across the board.

Players who have never beaten Tiger Woods have made vastly more money during their careers because of him. His presence made the tour more valuable for everyone.

Tiger didn't just win majors. He made the people who finished second more famous and more wealthy than the people who won majors before he arrived.

The Comebacks

What made Woods's story more than just a sporting achievement was what came after his peak. The knee surgeries, the back surgeries — four of them — the personal scandals, the years of struggling to break par on courses he had once dominated. And then the 2019 Masters, which he won at the age of 43, completing one of sport's most extraordinary comebacks.

The 2021 car accident that nearly cost him his leg seemed to end his competitive career. And yet Woods has continued to compete at major championships, absorbing pain that would have retired most players, driven by a relationship with the game that goes beyond rational calculation.

The Legacy

Rory McIlroy, Jon Rahm, Scottie Scheffler — the generation of players who grew up watching Tiger are now the best players in the world. All of them cite him as the reason they started playing golf seriously. His influence on who plays the game, how it is played, and how it is valued commercially will be felt for generations.
author: SportsKeen Editorial
